narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile for Year 3 performance, noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among accepted students. This weak academic standing in the later stage of your studies signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in the opposite direction. At 35.5, your score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction somewhat toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the concerns raised by your grades.

Your first-year academic performance ranked third. Placing in the third decile, well below the average of 6.0 among accepted applicants, added further weight toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently lower class rankings as the dominant signal that you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam, outweighing your solid but not exceptional LSAT.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving these two areas will directly address the factors that led to your rejection.
